definition: Deep, bitter resentment that lasts a long time.
example: Years after the dispute over the fence, rancor still soured every conversation between the two neighbors.
nuance: Anger can flare up and fade quickly, but rancor is bitterness that has hardened and lasts long after the original offense.
prompt: Two former business partners meet again ten years after a bitter split.
options: The rancor between the partners was still obvious when they refused to shake hands.
Full of rancor, she warmly thanked her old partner for all he had taught her.
Speaking with rancor, he frankly and fairly listed the mistakes they had both made.
The rancor of the stale coffee in the lobby made both partners wrinkle their noses.
reasons: Refusing a handshake a decade later shows a grudge that never healed.
Warm gratitude is the opposite of lingering bitterness.
This confuses the word with candor; fair, honest speech is not resentment.
This mixes the word up with rancid; it names a feeling, not a spoiled smell.

practice.prompt: A violinist is passed over for first chair in favor of a newer student.
options: Her rancor toward the newcomer lasted all season, and she rarely spoke to him.
Out of rancor, she baked him cookies to celebrate his well-earned new seat.
She practiced scales with such rancor that her technique grew precise and polished.
The rancor of the brass section was so loud that the violinists covered their ears.
reasons: A grudge that keeps her silent for months is the long-held bitterness the word names.
Celebrating a rival's success shows generosity, not resentment.
This treats the word as diligence or rigor, but it means bitterness, not hard work.
The word names an emotion, not a loud noise like a racket.
